title: The Lumières' 1895 Paris screening
description: On December 28, 1895, the Lumières projected short everyday-life films for a paying audience at the Grand Café in Paris, usually counted as cinema's birth; their light three-in-one Cinématographe traveled the world.

facts.text: On December 28, 1895, the Lumière brothers held a showing at the Grand Café on the boulevard des Capucines in Paris, which Britannica calls the beginning of cinema history.

title: Neorealism: cinema out of the rubble
description: After Fascism fell, Italian filmmakers shot on real, war-damaged streets with ordinary-looking casts, as in Rossellini's Open City.

facts.text: Italian Neorealism, rooted in the 1920s but held back for nearly two decades by Fascist control, emerged in great strength after the Fascist regime fell at the end of World War II.
Neorealist films had a documentary-like objectivity; their actors either were or looked like ordinary people involved in commonplace situations.
Roberto Rossellini's Open City (1945) was shot just months after the Allies liberated Rome, using the city's rubble-strewn streets and a cast many of whom were not actors.
The BFI reports that Open City was made on the streets of war-ravaged Rome with scraps of 35mm film stock.

title: Bicycle Thieves: real streets, real faces
description: De Sica's Bicycle Thieves (1948) told a small story of a poor man's stolen bicycle, shot on location with non-professional actors.

facts.text: Vittorio De Sica's Bicycle Thieves (1948), written by Cesare Zavattini, follows a poor man in postwar Rome whose bicycle, essential for his job, is stolen; he and his son search for it.
In Bicycle Thieves, Antonio's new job pasting posters on walls requires a bicycle.
Bicycle Thieves was shot on location with non-professional actors, Lamberto Maggiorani and Enzo Staiola, as the father and son.
De Sica was drawn to Lamberto Maggiorani's callused worker's hands and the way he moved, both of which signified his class.

title: The New Wave: critics become directors
description: Critics from Cahiers du cinéma, such as Truffaut and Godard, reacted against polished French films and began directing their own in the late 1950s.

facts.text: The New Wave was the style of highly individualistic French directors of the late 1950s, among them Claude Chabrol, François Truffaut, Alain Resnais and Jean-Luc Godard.
Many New Wave directors, including Truffaut and Godard, were associated with the film magazine Cahiers du cinéma, where they had written as critics in the 1950s.
For eight years at Cahiers du cinéma, Truffaut was the most truculent critic of contemporary French cinema, which he considered stale and conventional.
The New Wave was a reaction against the commercial production system: the well-constructed plot, the merely craftsmanlike approach and the French 'tradition of quality'.
Truffaut's semiautobiographical The 400 Blows (1959) won the best direction prize at the 1959 Cannes festival, establishing him as a leader of the New Wave.

title: Breathless: cheap tools become a style
description: Godard's Breathless was shot handheld on a low budget and cut with visible jump cuts that break continuity.

facts.text: Breathless (1960) used low-budget guerrilla techniques: cinematographer Raoul Coutard shot handheld and was once pushed in a wheelchair because the production could not afford tracks.
To shorten Breathless, Godard cut within scenes rather than removing whole ones, producing jump cuts that break continuity and draw attention to the filmmaking.
The New Wave helped demonstrate that films could achieve both commercial and artistic success.

title: Rashomon: one event, four versions
description: Kurosawa's Rashomon shows a single crime recalled differently by four people, a meditation on the nature of truth.

facts.text: Kurosawa Akira's Rashomon (1950), adapted from two Akutagawa stories, shows a rape and a murder recollected in distinctly different ways by four people: a samurai, his wife, a bandit and a woodcutter.

Showing the same event as seen by different people caught audiences' imagination and advanced the idea of cinema as a way to probe a deep philosophical problem; Britannica calls Rashomon a meditation on the nature of truth.

title: Rashomon's prize opens the West
description: Rashomon's Golden Lion at Venice in 1951 brought Japanese film serious attention worldwide.

facts.text: Rashomon won the Golden Lion, the top prize at the 1951 Venice Film Festival, the first time a Japanese film had won such high international acclaim.
After Rashomon's success, Japanese films attracted serious attention all over the world, and new export markets opened in the West.

title: Ozu's low, still camera
description: Ozu framed scenes low, as if seated on a tatami mat, barely moved the camera, avoided fades and dissolves, and used pillow shots between scenes.

facts.text: Ozu framed scenes from a low angle, as if seated on a tatami mat, used a 50mm lens exclusively and kept camera movement to a minimum.
Ozu almost totally abandoned devices such as camera movement in favour of straight pictorial shots.
In Tokyo Story, fades and dissolves are conspicuous by their absence, and tracking shots are rare.
Critic Noël Burch named Ozu's short, place-setting shots between scenes, of seas, mountains, boats, train tracks, buildings and rooms, 'pillow shots'; they keep his measured rhythm.

title: Ozu and the drama of ordinary families
description: Ozu's shomin-geki found drama in lower-middle-class family life, as in Tokyo Story's visit of an aged couple to their children.

facts.text: Ozu originated the shomin-geki, 'common-people's drama', a genre about lower-middle-class Japanese family life.
Tokyo Story (1953) follows an aged couple on their first trip to Tokyo, from their seaside hometown of Onomichi, to visit the families of their two eldest children.

title: Ray learns from neorealism
description: Satyajit Ray, an advertising art director and book designer, was inspired by Bicycle Thieves to film on location with non-professionals.

facts.text: Before filmmaking, Satyajit Ray worked as an art director at a British advertising agency and became a leading Indian typographer and book-jacket designer.
Ray illustrated an edition of Bibhutibhushan Banerjee's novel Pather Panchali, whose possibilities as a film began to intrigue him.
Ray was inspired by De Sica's The Bicycle Thief, which showed a film could be made on location with non-professional actors; meeting Jean Renoir in Bengal in 1949 also encouraged him.

title: Pather Panchali brings realism to Indian film
description: Ray's Pather Panchali (1955), made against the odds, gave a naturalistic portrait of a poor Bengal village family and won at Cannes.

facts.text: Bengali producers distrusted Ray's unconventional approach, so he began shooting in late 1952 with his own money and an inexperienced crew; with reluctant help from the West Bengal government, the film took two and a half years.

Pather Panchali follows a boy, Apu, growing up in an impoverished rural community in Bengal; in one of its most memorable scenes, Apu and his sister run through a paddy field to glimpse a passing train.
The BFI describes Pather Panchali as a naturalistic portrait of ordinary lives in a rural family, with all its mischief, discoveries, joys and tragedies.
Pather Panchali (1955) was a commercial and critical success and won a major award at the 1956 Cannes festival, which let Ray make the rest of the Apu trilogy.

title: Why Hindi films sing
description: Song and dance, inherited from Parsi theatre and present since the first talkie in 1931, run through every genre of popular Hindi film and drive box office.

facts.text: Sound arrived in Indian cinema in 1931 with the first talkie, the Hindi-language Alam Ara.
Alam Ara was advertised as 'All talking, all singing, all dancing' and contained seven song sequences.
Parsi theatre, which flourished between the 1850s and 1930s, was a forerunner to Bollywood, combining folk and musical theatre traditions.
Bollywood, a blend of 'Bombay' and 'Hollywood', names the Hindi-language film industry.
Unlike Hollywood, where the musical is one genre, Bollywood puts song and dance into any and all of its other genres.
In Bollywood, film soundtracks and choreographed set pieces are often the engines that drive box-office results.

title: Playback singing
description: Playback singers prerecord film songs and the stars lip-sync to them on screen.

facts.text: Playback singers prerecord a film's songs, and the stars lip-sync to them on screen; the singers themselves do not appear.
Lata Mangeshkar, an iconic Indian playback singer, recorded songs for the soundtracks of more than 2,000 Indian films.

title: Bruce Lee and realistic kung fu
description: Bruce Lee's realistic, fast martial arts made Hong Kong action famous, and Enter the Dragon joined Hong Kong and U.S. producers.

facts.text: Bruce Lee's first Hong Kong films, The Big Boss (1971) and Fist of Fury (1972), were huge successes; audiences embraced The Big Boss's realistic martial arts.
The speed of Lee's punches and the fluidity of his kicks, rooted in rigorous training, gave his films a fresh sense of authenticity and realism.
Enter the Dragon (1973), the first joint venture between Hong Kong- and U.S.-based production companies, was a worldwide hit; Lee died on July 20, 1973, before its release.

title: Opera training, stunts and wirework
description: Peking opera training shaped Jackie Chan and Yuen Woo-ping, whose comedy, real stunts and wirework reshaped action filmmaking worldwide.

facts.text: From age 7 to 17, Jackie Chan studied acrobatics, singing, martial arts and mime at a strict boarding school that trained students for Peking opera.
Yuen Woo-ping was born into a family of Peking Opera performers, a tradition in which drama, martial arts, acrobatics and dance were inseparable.
In 1978 Jackie Chan found his signature bumbling physical comedy in Snake in the Eagle's Shadow and Drunken Master, Yuen Woo-ping's first two films as director.
Jackie Chan is known for performing his own dangerous stunts; a fall while filming Armour of God (1986) fractured his skull.
Yuen Woo-ping's work on The Matrix (1999), combining Hong Kong wirework (harnesses and cables that propel and suspend performers) with science fiction, changed how Hollywood approaches action.

title: Why Nigerian film turned to video
description: The naira's fall in the 1980s made film equipment scarce and theaters hard to reach, and celluloid production stopped.

facts.text: In the 1980s the devaluation of the Nigerian naira made film equipment hard to come by and movie theaters increasingly inaccessible; by the early 1990s celluloid film production had ceased.

title: Nollywood: an industry on videotape
description: Living in Bondage (1992) went straight to VHS, launching a fast, low-budget video industry later nicknamed Nollywood.

facts.text: Britannica dates Nigeria's video film industry to 1992 and Living in Bondage, which was distributed straight to VHS, became a smash hit and revolutionized Nigerian cinema.
Nollywood films were largely low-budget, and most were shot in about a week.
Nollywood includes films in Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa and other languages of Nigeria.
The word 'Nollywood', from Nigeria and Hollywood, first appeared in a New York Times headline in 2002.

title: Venice and Cannes
description: Venice (1932) is the oldest film festival; Cannes, planned for 1939, opened in 1946. Their prizes make films known abroad.

facts.text: The Venice Film Festival, founded in 1932 and officially part of the Venice Biennale, is the world's oldest film festival; its top prize is the Golden Lion.
Cannes began as Philippe Erlanger's idea for an event to replace Venice's festival and offer the world a festival free of pressure and constraints.
The first Cannes festival was to open on 1 September 1939, the day Germany invaded Poland; it finally took place in 1946.
Cannes awarded its first Palme d'Or in 1955, to Delbert Mann's Marty.
The main auditorium of Cannes's Palais des Festivals bears the name of cinema pioneer Louis Lumière and hosts the Festival de Cannes ceremonies.

title: Festivals as marketplaces
description: At Cannes, producers and distributors view films and sign contracts; its Marché du Film became official in 1959.

facts.text: Cannes became an international marketplace where producers and distributors could exchange ideas, view films and sign contracts.
The Marché du Film, the Cannes film market held unofficially since 1946, was given official status in 1959.

title: Go-betweens carry films across borders
description: People and festivals carried films abroad: Stramigioli sent Rashomon to Venice, and Open City won at the first Cannes.

facts.text: Italifilm president Giuliana Stramigioli recommended Rashomon to the selection committee in Venice, where it won the Golden Lion in 1951.
Open City won the Grand Prix at Cannes, the top prize at the first festival, in 1946.
